title: The Well at Kamlapur

setup.context: Let me tell you about the well in Kamlapur. It nearly never got fixed.

paragraphs.text: Kamlapur is a village about four hours from the city, along a road that floods every monsoon. The main well went dry when I was in my forties. The women walked two kilometres for water after that, twice a day, for years.
Nobody in the village thought a stranger from the city could change that. I didn't either. I had written letters to the panchayat, and they had written back, politely, that the file was with someone.

So I did what I should have done first. I sat in the courtyard every evening for a month and listened. The old men talked about the water table. The girls talked about school hours that moved with the walk to the well.
We cleared the old shaft together. It took eleven weekends and more blisters than I can count. The engineer from the district came once and said it would never hold. It held.
The water came back in the second monsoon. Nobody made a speech. Mrs. Savitri filled a pot, carried it home, and then went back for a second one, just to be sure.
It isn't a victory I can put on a stage. It's a well that works, which is more than most of my speeches ever did.

reflection.insight: Ideas spread on talk. Things change when people do the work next to each other. Most of what I know about urgency came from that courtyard, not from a book.
reflection.question: Is there something near you that everyone has learned to walk around?

follow_up_options: What happened to the engineer's prediction?
Did the village keep it going?
Why did you stop writing letters?

responses_to_follow_ups.engineer: He came back a year later, looked at the shaft, and asked who had designed it. The answer was a retired carpenter named Jairam who had never built a well in his life and had simply refused to give up on the idea.
responses_to_follow_ups.kept_going: Yes. They set up a rota for cleaning the shaft after each monsoon, and the girls keep a notebook of the water level. It is not my project anymore, and that is the point.
responses_to_follow_ups.letters: I still write them. But I write them after I have sat in a courtyard, not before. The letters are better that way, and so are the answers.
